articles.summary: Answers for some frequent questions about Radiance interactions.

details.title: RADIANCE RULES FAQ AND CLARIFICATIONS
details.tagline: Answers for some frequent questions about Radiance interactions.
paragraphs: Welcome to the Radiance FAQ article! As mentioned in the Radiance Release Notes article, the FAQ article serves as a collection of rulings and clarifications at our usual cadence, and serves as an additional supplemental article to the Release Notes article.

The FAQ is a collection of official rulings. In places where the FAQ differs from the Core Rules Document, the FAQ takes precedence. When a new Core Rules Document is released, it will take precedence over any points that differ from this document.
Throughout this document, we use some specific shorthand to represent symbols in card text. Here’s a short guide:
[C] means “one power of this card’s domain”
[C] in Accelerate costs takes on the domain of the Unit, or turns into [A] if the Unit has no domain or multiple domains.
[C] in other cases is treated as the corresponding power symbol in all respects, matching how the cards are actually printed—it’s just a design shorthand!
If my opponent empowers Kharox and chooses to play my Neeko, Blending In from my trash with the triggered ability, do they get one of the Legends I chose during deckbuilding?

When the play effect of the Neeko played through Kharox resolves, if their deck has one or more copies of Neeko, Blending In, they can add one of the Legends they chose during deckbuilding to their Legend Zone as if they had played a copy of Neeko that they own. The Legends they add to the Legend Zone don’t have any relation to the Legends their opponent chose. If their deck has no copies of Neeko, in the Main Deck or the sideboard, that instruction will be ignored.
If I play Mobilize while I control Seraphic Wyvern and I only have one rune left in my Rune Deck, do I still draw a card?

Referencing the action in this way refers only to the game action and the game object it was performed on. The channel event that Seraphic Wyvern instructs introduces a new game object that the action is performed on, but the referenced action is still only the original one in the instructions of the spell.

The same logic applies to Catalyst of Aeons played while its controller has a Seraphic Wyvern on the board and only two runes left in their Rune Deck. They were able to channel 2 runes, even if the additional game object instructed to be channeled by Seraphic Wyvern wasn’t possible. Therefore they will not draw 1.
If I play Meticulous Restorationist from my trash for [Y] via its triggered ability, can I banish a unit or gear from my trash with Mordekaiser, Iron Revenant to pay the cost?
“Play me for [Cost]” is an alternate cost which replaces the base cost ([2]) with the alternate cost ([Y]). Mordekaiser, Iron Revenant’s Power can only be spent to play units.
If I play Atakhan and kill a non-token unit for its additional cost, can I banish that unit with Mordekaiser, Iron Revenant to help pay for Atakhan’s Power cost?

When paying costs in Riftbound, you pay Energy and Power costs before you perform other “non-standard” costs, like Atakhan’s optional additional cost to kill a unit. When paying the Power cost of Atakhan, the unit in question is not actually dead yet, and thus cannot be banished from your trash.
If I kill Runeblade Anvil during an opponent’s turn, when is the last moment I can play the banished card?
You can play it until the Ending Phase in your next turn begins.
If I kill Runeblade Anvil during my turn, can I play the card during the Ending Phase of that turn?
The duration for Runeblade Anvil’s permission is “until your next Ending Phase.” It is valid until the specified point in the specified turn begins, and then the permission is lost.
If I kill Runeblade Anvil during my Ending Phase, when is the last moment I can play the banished card?
You can play it until the Ending Phase in your next turn begins.
Your next Ending Phase after your current Ending Phase is the one in your next turn. Until that Ending Phase begins, you will be able to play the card in question.
If I control Hunters’ Circle and I play Baron Nashor without a Baron Pit on the board, can I play him for [9][C][C][C]?

Hunters’ Circle applies a cost reduction to the first unit or gear each player plays there during their turn. Baron Nashor entering at the Baron Pit is a replacement effect that applies while Baron resolves and enters the board. In comparison, Hunters’ Circle’s cost reduction is in effect during finalization, when choosing play locations in step 2 and determining the total cost in step 3. By the time Baron Nashor’s replacement effect applies, his cost has been determined and paid.
If I control a battlefield and I have Riven, the Exile as my legend, can I play Baron Nashor without a Baron Pit on the board and have him enter ready?

Riven, the Exile applies a replacement effect to units her controller plays to a battlefield they control. This refers to step 2 of finalization, when players pick the play location for a unit they are playing. Riven then generates a replacement effect for those units, which causes them to enter ready. When Baron Nashor enters in this scenario, there are two replacement effects that apply to the event of him entering: him entering ready, and him entering to the Baron Pit. Regardless of the order of these replacement effects, Baron Nashor will enter ready at the Baron Pit.
For Riven, Broken Blade’s exhaust trigger, do I spend the buff when finalizing the triggered ability or when it resolves?

A cost within instructions that doesn’t appear as the first part of a triggered ability’s effect is part of the instructions that occur on resolution and not the base cost of the triggered ability. The first part of Riven, Broken Blade’s triggered ability is “Choose one that hasn’t been chosen this turn…”
If I Standard Move a Riven, Broken Blade and a Stellacorn Herder simultaneously, which goes on the chain first: Riven’s exhaust trigger or Stellacorn Herder’s move trigger?

The order of the triggers on the chain after the move event completes is: exhaust triggers first, followed by move triggers. The cost to perform the move occurs before the move action is actually performed.
If I attempt to Standard Move to a battlefield with Gravity Field and decline the cost, can I still exhaust my unit?

The Standard Move is an inherent ability. We’ll clarify some established consensus on how the Standard Move operates: you cannot attempt to perform the Standard Move if the resulting move is not possible, nor if you cannot pay its associated costs.

Additionally, if the Standard Move incurs a Cost that cannot be paid, or if the move action cannot otherwise be performed, the Standard Move and all actions taken as part of performing it will be undone, any effects those actions caused to occur are similarly undone, and the Standard Move will be cancelled.
If I play Charm moving an enemy unit to a battlefield where I control Gravity Field, does its controller have to pay the cost?
The opponent must pay [1][A] to move a unit to the battlefield with Gravity Field, but Charm instructs you to move the enemy unit and not your opponent.
If your opponent controlled the Gravity Field at that battlefield, you would be the one who would have to pay [1][A] to move the enemy unit to that battlefield when Charm resolves.
What about if I play Angler Wyrm’s activated ability while it’s located at the same battlefield with Gravity Field? Will they have to pay the cost to move the unit to the battlefield?
Unlike Charm, Angler Wyrm instructs your opponent to move their unit, so they must pay the cost in order to move it to that battlefield. If they choose not to or can’t, the unit does not move.

Speaking of Angler Wyrm, if my opponent plays Angler Wyrm’s activated ability choosing me and I play Hunker Down on one of my units, can I pick that unit when Angler Wyrm instructs me to move a unit even if I control other units?

The chosen opponent must perform the move game action if they have a unit that can move. If they control some number of units that cannot move, they cannot choose to “move” those units to satisfy the move instructions, as no move is actually possible. If they control no units that can move, the instruction is negated. If they have some number of units that can move, they must move one of those units.
If I play Possession and take control of my opponent’s Ekko, Revolutionary, can I play his activated ability to banish and then play him? Do I control him when he comes back in?

details.title: RIFTBOUND 2027 PREMIER PLAY
details.tagline: An overview of the revamped Premier Play program for 2027.
paragraphs: August’s State of Play gave a high-level overview of the types of events that make up our 2027 Organized Play program. Today’s article is a behemoth with a lot of information about the updates to Riftbound’s play systems.
Here’s a quick summary of what’s in this article:
Riftbound Organized Play is continuing to grow in 2027!
Riftbound is getting a ranked ladder in 2027, and our top players of each year will earn the “Grandmaster” title.
Our four Continentals in 2027 are in Dallas, Melbourne, London, and Toronto.
Winners of Challenge Series events will earn a free competitor badge to a Regional.
You can earn a competitor badge and qualify for Day 2 of Continentals through consistent top finishes at tournaments, even if they don’t earn a badge or invite directly from those tournaments.

There is a lot in this article—the above five things just scratch the surface. This article is one part primer on the system and one part introductory policy document. We’ve opted to go in-depth here to fully explain each change.
There is also a recurring point in this article that things are not finalized. We’re estimating our status to be… roughly 92.6%. What is that number based on? Nothing scientific.

Part of the reason for this is because the Organized Play program is made up of a lot of separate parts and systems that all work together. For example, this article talks about how you can qualify for specific events, which means we have to get into both the events they can qualify for and the events they play in to earn that qualification.

Given the size of this article, we broke out a separate article to talk specifically about the Nexus Cup & Challenge Series tournaments. That article also includes more details about the plans to sunset Summoner Skirmish, and what you can do with any byes they’ve earned but don’t plan to use at Regionals next year. We’ll discuss Challenge Series here as well, but mainly with respect to how it connects to the larger play program.
Now, before diving in: if you’d like a refresher, here’s a reminder about our core philosophy for Riftbound Organized Play. Skip ahead to the next section if you want to get right into the changes.

details.title: RIFTBOUND 2027 LOCAL PLAY
details.tagline: The revamped 2027 Local Play program, including Nexus Cups, Challenge Series, and unused Byes.
paragraphs: With Legacy on the horizon, we're taking a deeper dive into the upcoming programs for you to join at your local game store. As Riftbound grows and we have seen more about how you play and want to play, we will re-evaluate and improve our play programs.

Our vision for Riftbound play is to build two play programs which help us serve the different types of players in Riftbound: a Competitive ladder that serves players striving to compete and a separate structure that we've cleverly named 'Fun-petitive' to provide a structure that rewards players for being active at their local game stores and is less about the drive to win and more about the drive to socialize and participate.
At the core, good play programs are about incentivizing and rewarding players for playing the way they want to play, and we feel Riftbound is served best by building both of these tracks.

This isn't to say these are two separate pools of players. While you may be drawn to one or the other, there are certainly times the streams will cross, and you will be able to play in both. Good communities thrive on the diversity of their players.

Pre-Rift events will remain a staple of our play programs. The Legacy Pre-Rifts will kick off January 22, 2026, and run through January 28, 2026. Pre-Rifts will fall primarily in the Fun-petitive side of the play programs, but we have no doubt players who are driven by mastery will join alongside players who are looking to just hang and play some card games.

Compare this to the soon-to-be sunset Summoner Skirmish program. As we shared in the State of Play article, this program was found to be in an awkward position. It had great promos and cool playmats our social players wanted to chase, but also Byes that our most competitive players were driven to farm. The mixed incentives, combined with the challenges we outlined around the bye-reward program, led us to rethink our store programs and land on the new Nexus Cup & Challenge Series programs.
With the announcement of Summoner Skirmish's coming retirement, we shared that we were working on plans for any unused Byes that you earned but were unable to use. We've got that update for you here.

If you have any unused Summoner Skirmish byes you will be able to redeem them at any Regional in 2027. You can do so by contacting UVS after registering for the event and emailing OP@uvsgames.com. The UVS support team will be able to implement this bye for you ahead of the event. Emails must be sent no later than 14 days prior to the start of the event. You can also implement the bye on-site at the event when you pick up your badge, ahead of the start of the main event.

If you cannot, or do not want to redeem any earned byes, we will be offering to replace them with a promo from Set 7, The Reckoning. We will be sharing it with players in the future when we open the redemption for this promo next year.
We'll be back with more information about how it will work as we get closer, but we do have answers for some of your most important questions about this program now:
Byes will be redeemed 1-for-1 with the promo (multiple byes receive multiple promos).
This promo will only be available via this redemption program.
Redemptions will need to be completed by December 31, 2027, at 11:59:59pm Pacific.
Now, on to the new programs launching in January with Legacy.

Nexus Cup asks the question "Who's the local champion?" This is a per-set event at LGS aimed at crowning your store's best. The Nexus Cup doesn't feed up into the competitive programs; it's about local recognition and bragging rights.
While we did reveal the promo from The Reckoning, we aren't going to be revealing any Legacy promos today. What we can share is that the prizing for Nexus Cup will look like the following:
Prizing will look familiar to Summoner Skirmish players in that the promos will be:
Winner & Top 8 promos - Sharing the same card, with unique stamps to denote the placement
Participation promos - A unique promo for players who compete in the event.
As we note in the other article today about the play programs, we are working on a 'Fun-petitive' play program, we'll share more details on that in the future.

This is a per-set program which will be available to select Riftbound Gaming Network stores. As this directly feeds into the competitive ladder, we want to maintain a certain bar for stores to meet to qualify to run these events so as to give players the best experience and minimize issues as they begin their ascent up the ranked ladder.

If you haven't read it yet, be sure to read the other article today as it will give a much deeper overview of the competitive program, introduce Ladder Points, and dive into the benefits it affords as players rise in the ranks. We won't delve deeply into the details of it here, but here's a quick introduction.

Ladder Points are the points players earn as part of competitive Riftbound events. Ladder Points raise your rank on the Ladder, and each rank awards you benefits. You earn Ladder Points based on your finish in competitive events. Challenge Series award Ladder Points if you finish in the Top 32 of the event.
As 2026 made clear, many of you are hungry for the competitive challenges of Riftbound, and the Challenge Series is to help fill that demand.
Challenge Series events will award both promos and Challenge Points to competitors. For the launch of this series the rewards will look as follows:
These promos will be of the same card with unique stamps to denote a winner vs a Top 8 finisher. As with the Nexus Cup, we aren't ready to reveal the promo for this yet, hang in there.

Since we're sharing a great deal about the organized player programs for 2027 in this and the other article, we know you have questions and the community will raise issues to address. Stay tuned for updates or follow-ups based on the community conversations.
If you want to understand more about the larger program, Ladder Points, the ranked ladder and more - learn more in the other article today.
Keep an eye out in the coming weeks for stores to begin listing these events so you can register and compete as part of Legacy in 2027!

articles.title: Testing Start of Game Rules
articles.summary: We’re testing out some rule adjustments to equalize win rates between going first and second.

details.title: TESTING START OF GAME RULES
details.tagline: We’re testing out some rule adjustments to equalize win rates between going first and second.
headings: Is this a rules update? Do I have to follow the stuff in this article at my Nexus Night, or in my next match at Regionals?
So, what are the changes you’re testing?
What does this look like in practice?
When will the playtested rules actually be in effect globally?
paragraphs: We’ve had an exciting first year of Riftbound, and we’ve learned a lot within the last year. One thing hasn't changed—we’re committed to adapting to make the game better and more engaging for everybody.

With that said, going first in turn order currently has a higher win rate than we would like, and along with the upcoming templating and rules overhaul planned for Legacy, we want to further improve the Riftbound playing experience by potentially making some adjustments here as well. We’ve landed on three possible changes that will get us closer to a 50% win rate split between going first and second.
In order to evaluate which solution is best, we’ll be testing some new rules at events worldwide (outside of premier tournaments).
Is this a rules update? Do I have to follow the stuff in this article at my Nexus Night, or in my next match at Regionals?
No. Right now, we’re playtesting changes at select events to even out the win rate between going first vs. going second.
Some of these changes may be finalized as part of Riftbound’s core ruleset, but we’re looking to get more data on which of our possible solutions works best before we make that call.
So, what are the changes you’re testing?

The current problem: going first in turn order has a higher win rate than we would like. This means that channeling an extra Rune—our current bonus for going second in turn order, or “go-second advantage”—isn’t enough of a boost to balance out the inherent advantage of going first.
Here’s what we’ll be testing to address this. Again, this is just a test for now. We’ll determine what changes make it to Riftbound’s actual ruleset after testing is finished.
We’re changing turn order decisions to occur before Battlefields are selected. After battlefields are selected, sideboarding occurs if applicable, and then Battlefields are revealed.
We want the choice to go first or second to be a solid commitment before your opponent's Battlefield is disclosed.
In best-of-threes you will now be able to make every battlefield choice with the knowledge of who is going first or second.
In best-of-one battlefield selection will remain random, but you will know which of your battlefields was selected before sideboarding. Your opponent’s will be revealed after sideboarding.

This means sideboarding decisions can be made with full knowledge of your turn order and your battlefield. This eliminates the added layer of considering your card selection and battlefield without knowing whether or not your opponent will choose to go first or second in the latter rounds of a best-of-three.

We’re adding another perk to the go-second advantage. While playtesting these new rules, the player who goes second will get one of the following, in addition to channeling three Runes on their first turn:
They will start at 1 point. Or,
They will draw an extra card. Or,
They will predict before their first draw.

Basically, we’re investigating whether card advantage, card quality, or points will most impact the win rate on going first vs. going second. Event staff will communicate clearly before each event whether A, B, or C will be tested.
Each of these proposed solutions has their own advantages and disadvantages, and we’d love to break down some of the thoughts behind each of them.

The core disadvantage to going second is that you’re behind on point-scoring opportunities. In this world, the first player would start the game ahead on board development because they take the first turn, but the second player would be ahead on points as a counterbalance. This is the most extreme change that we’re interested in, but we think it’s valuable to test a change that directly interacts with the scoring system that is central to the going first advantage.

Having more cards than your opponent is an advantage in a card game, and many card games give an extra card to the player who goes second. This makes it more likely that the second player has the card they need when they need it, and the extra material also gives them an advantage in games that go long and come down to attrition.

We explored the idea of taking away the first player’s draw on their first turn, but ultimately decided it would create too large of a change in how players needed to build their decks. Giving the second player an extra card draw keeps deckbuilding incentives fairly similar and rhymes nicely with giving them an extra Rune, so we’ve chosen to test this version.

This is a softer version of the previous rule. If getting a whole extra card is too much, we think it could be enough to let the second player control their first draw based on their opponent’s choice of Battlefield and first turn play. We think that the whole extra card is a more straightforward solution, but this is an alternative that we’d like to test in case the extra card ends up being too strong.
What does this look like in practice?

Here’s how you’ll start your games if you’re in a playtest session. (Also, with these proposed rules, the start of game procedure will be more closely aligned between best-of-one and best-of-three formats.)
Decide which player will go first or second.
Select Battlefields, and place them facedown.
Sideboard (in the second and third games).
Going first player channels 2, and draws 1.
Going second player channels 3. Then they Predict 1, or draw an extra card, or start with 1 point. (New)
Decide which player will go first or second.
Look at your own Battlefield, keeping it hidden from the opponent. (New)
Going first player channels 2, and draws 1.
Going second player channels 3. Then they Predict 1, or draw an extra card, or start with 1 point. (New)
In both best-of-one and best-of-three, you will now be able to sideboard with the knowledge of your own Battlefield and turn order, but not your opponent’s Battlefield.
We’ll be testing these adjustments at events worldwide outside of our premier tournaments. You can expect to see playtests at:
Radiance season City Tournaments in China.
Friday and Sunday Standard Challenges at the upcoming European Regional Championship in Stuttgart.
We’ll be in touch with tournament officials about the logistics, and the rules being tested will be communicated to all participants attending the events.

If you are interested in testing these rules out in local or casual games, we encourage you to do so! We’ve got eyes across the community, and will monitor conversation and feedback. That said, you’re not required to change anything about the way you play until we make an official rules update. Skirmishes, Showdowns and other high OPL events should not playtest these rules unless directly communicated to Tournament Organizers.

Testing rules changes at larger scale events gives us a much bigger pool of data to work from. With way more players testing these changes, we can get a much better idea of which solutions bring us closer to a 50% win rate split between going first and second.
Beyond the numbers, we want to make sure these proposed solves feel good to play with as well, and that’s where your feedback comes in!
When will the playtested rules actually be in effect globally?
We’re planning to analyze and dive deeper into the data from the Radiance season to make a decision leading into the launch of our sixth set, Legacy.

You can expect an official rules adjustment (or an announcement that there will be no changes) to be included in our Patch Notes for Legacy, along with our reasoning and findings. The community is incredibly important to us, and as we make these changes to help Riftbound grow, we’re excited to bring everyone along for the ride and include your input to help make the game we all love even better.

details.tagline: Adjustments to Regional Championship prizing and policy.
paragraphs: We are less than one month away from the European Regional Championship, taking place in Stuttgart, Germany, and we want to update competitors with:
Changes to prizing plans for Regional Championship events, including how Overnumber Foil Plated Legends are being awarded.
Updates to the Competitive Integrity Policy for Regional Championship events.
A brief look at the 2026 Riftbound World Championship Showcase event.

When we introduced Best-Of prizing in Houston, it quickly became an exciting part of competitive Riftbound. As players moved from Regional Qualifiers to Regional Championships, we wanted the rewards to grow alongside the level of competition, leading us to introduce Overnumbered Foil Plated Legends as Regional Championship Best-Of prizes.

Since then, we’ve been tracking how these rewards influence competitive decisions beyond simply encouraging players to represent their favorite Legends. After discussing the role we want these prizes to play in Riftbound, we’re making the following adjustments to Regional Championship prizing:
Overnumbered Foil Plated Legends will now reward overall tournament performance.
The top 58 finishers will draft from the available Overnumbered Foil Plated Legends in finishing order, beginning with 1st place and continuing until all 58 Legends have been selected.
Foil Plated Legends from Unleashed, Vendetta, and Radiance will become the new Best-Of rewards. These will be awarded to the highest finishing eligible player on their respective Legend.
Origins, Proving Grounds, and Spiritforged Legends will not be eligible for Foil Plated Legend Best-Of prizing at Regional Championships.
Players must still advance to Day 2 on their Legend to qualify for a Best-Of Foil Plated Legend.

These Best-Of Foil Plated Legends are the same versions offered through Regional Qualifiers. Due to the timing of this adjustment, Radiance Foil Plated Legends will not be available for distribution at these events. We are currently determining the best way to deliver them to their recipients and expect them to become available in January 2027.
We believe these changes ultimately better reward competitors and incentivize the type of competition we want to see as part of Regional Championship Tournaments.
In addition to the above changes to prizing, we are taking some more steps to further the competitive integrity of Regional Championships. Here are the rules updates:
No Throwing Matches: Players may not ask for or offer match concessions at any point before or during these tournaments except in the cases outlined below.
No Deciding Matches After Time: If a match naturally ends in a draw due to time limits, players cannot attempt to randomly or arbitrarily determine a winner.
Open Decklists: Regional Championships will be played with open decklists.

Tournament Rule 401.5.b. states that tournaments with a professional OPL can be run with open decklists. We will be requiring this for these tournaments and want players to know this ahead of the events, and more importantly, ahead of when they need to lock their decklists.
We understand that certain situations require flexibility in the above. The following situations remain permitted:

Tactical Game Concessions: Players may concede individual games within a match for strategic reasons (such as preserving time for Game 3). But they may not tactically concede a match-determining game.
Legitimate Extenuating Circumstances: Players facing genuine external circumstances, such as medical emergencies, may yield a match.
Intentional Draws (IDs): Intentional Draws prior to time expiring remain legal and permitted under standard tournament policy.
We will be reiterating these rules before each event, including in email to competitors and through tournament floor announcements.

Players are expected to play each match to the best of their ability with the intention of winning the match. Any player found asking for, offering, or executing illegal match concessions or collusion agreements will face immediate disqualification from the event and potential suspension from competitive Riftbound play.

Lastly, we know that Overnumbered Foil Plated Legend cards have been the main motivation for many competitors at Regional Championships. With the 2026 Riftbound World Championship Showcase Event, the highest-level players will have something new to set their sights on, and Regional events are a crucial stepping stone to crowning our first World Champion.

The Top 8 of each Regional Championship (Europe, North America, and China) will be invited to compete in Riftbound’s first World Championship Showcase event, taking place at the end of January in China. If someone manages the impressive feat of making Top 8 at multiple Regional Championships, any invitations earned beyond their first will be passed down to the next eligible finisher of the relevant tournament.
We will share more about the World Showcase and what players will be competing for in future updates!

details.title: PREPARING FOR THE RADIANCE PRE-RIFT
details.tagline: Get ready to play Riftbound’s newest set at your local Pre-Rift.
paragraphs: This Friday, October 16, stores will begin running their Radiance Pre-Rift events.

Events begin on Friday, but the Pre-Rift window lasts for the week, so check the schedule at your local store to find out when you can register to play. If you want to see when local game stores are running Pre-Rifts near you, check out our event locator.

A Pre-Rift event is your first chance to get your hands on a new set’s cards and play with them before the set is officially released. When you attend a Pre-Rift, you get to crack packs with your local game store (LGS) community, build a deck, and play it immediately.

Pre-Rift events are fun, social, and casual! The focus is on learning and lighthearted fun, so don’t worry about bumping into any extreme competition. Instead, have fun with the people around you, chat about the deck you’re gonna try out, and don’t hesitate to ask your fellow Riftbounders or the event judge for help while you’re building your deck or in the middle of a game.

The other great thing about Pre-Rifts is that they are Sealed events. This means all the cards you need to play will be provided to you as part of the event, and you’ll just need to build your deck from that limited card pool.

In Sealed formats, you open Booster Packs and play with the cards you get; for this event, they'll be Radiance Booster Packs. You can use any of the cards you open from those packs when building your deck, but you can’t add outside cards from your collection to your deck.
If this is your first Sealed event, here are the deckbuilding rules to keep in mind:
Sealed decks have a minimum Main Deck size of 25 cards, but you can play more than that if you want to.
Sealed decks can use up to three domains of cards and Runes.
You can use any Signature spell in your deck, as long as both of that Signature spell’s domains are represented in your Main Deck’s three domains.
You can choose to play without a Legend, or without a Champion Unit. If you do, you draw an additional card on your first turn.
If you choose to play with a Legend, you must have both of the Legend’s domains represented in your Main Deck’s three domains.
You can use any Champion Unit as your Chosen Champion, regardless of your Legend.
You can use as many copies of a card as you open.
This means you can go above the normal limit of 3 copies per card.
You are not limited to using Runes or tokens that you open in your packs.
The event organizer will provide additional Runes, and you can use anything handy to represent tokens!
You can use Battlefields that you open, or use a facedown card as a "blank" substitute Battlefield. These blank Battlefields have no abilities and are just locations for players to conquer and hold.
You can change the cards of your deck in between games and rounds, as long as you’re still following the other rules above. Don’t be afraid to alter your build as you go!
For more details on Sealed deckbuilding, see the Tournament Rules.
For Radiance Pre-Rift events, you’ll be provided with the following to open and use to build your deck. Remember, anything you open is yours to keep!
A champion pack themed around one of nine new Legends in Radiance. These packs have a Legend, a Rare Champion, a Battlefield, and support cards all for that Champion.
A Heimerdinger, Academy Instructor promo card. You can’t include the Heimerdinger Promo in your Sealed deck. If you pull the non-promo version in your packs, you can play that one!
Remember, your Main Deck has to have at least 25 cards and follow the Domain rules listed above. With that in mind, here are a few tips for building your Sealed deck at a Pre-Rift:
Include a reasonable amount of Units in your deck, because they’re  your main way to score points.
Most decks want to have at least 15 Units that can fight for you.
You’ll want about five of your Units to cost 2 Energy, so you have plays to make in your first turns.
The rest of your Units can be more expensive, with a diversity of costs so you have powerful plays at all points of the game.
Use your non-Unit cards to help bolster the strategy of your deck.
Gear or Spells that give Might are great options to improve your Units.
It’s also always a good idea to have a few spells that will let you interact directly with your opponent’s Units by removing them from play.
Think about the different Power costs in your deck.
Cards with Power costs tend to have stronger effects, and you will want to have some without going overboard on the Runes you'll have to recycle.
When deciding what Runes to play in your Rune Deck, make sure to think about the specific Power costs in your Main Deck.
Radiance has new mechanics called Disarm, Deploy, and Show Off.
Try playing around with the new keywords to learn how they work.
When building the foundation of your deck, the cards from your Pre-Rift kit are a great place to start. Here's a quick rundown on the Champions in the Pre-Rift kits and their strategies.
Ekko is all about planning ahead, and manipulating time. Use his Legend to cheat out powerful units with impactful effects ahead of the curve.
Evelynn is all about luring you into her embrace and springing her trap. She uses hidden cards to outwit her enemies.

Jarvan IV leverages the new keyword Deploy. With his Legend, you can send Units to battlefields with Deployed Gear and surprise your opponent, getting Units directly into the fight even if your base is empty. You can’t count Jarvan out of the fight.

K’Sante is all about protecting his allies and Battlefields. His unique flavor is that he can transform his defenses to be used on offense. Surprise your opponents by turning your beefy Hold cards into Conquering monsters.
Mordekaiser rules over the realm of death. His game plan centers around banishing his own Gear and Units, to play out more Units and Gear for cheaper.

Orianna’s Legend puts a new spin on Riftbound. She can transform powerful Gear into powerful Units, and even surprise opponents by transforming Deployed Gear into a Unit at unexpected times. Use your robot army to conquer Battlefields from underneath the opponent’s nose.

Riven is an exiled swordfighter who focuses on movement, and her Legend leans into this game plan. Allowing Units that are played to the Battlefield to come in ready synergises with cards that can Gank or have exhaust abilities, creating a surprising amount of early game pressure.

Seraphine draws powers from her followers, and can exhaust them to help her cast expensive, game-changing spells. Her game plan is to assemble a large army of low cost Units and overwhelm her opponent with both spells and sheer numbers.

Ziggs is a chaotic yordle who wants to blow everything up—and he really wants to blow up the board. His game plan leans fully into controlling the board and deterring the enemy from even setting foot on a Battlefield.

If you haven't, check out our recently released patch notes. We’ll be releasing an extended FAQ once Radiance has been out for a bit to cover any odd interactions, but we wanted to call out a few things early to make Pre-Rift as smooth as possible.
Q: If I use K’Sante Legend on a Unit like Staunch Survivor that has both Shield 2 and Assault 2, does the card now have Assault 4?

A: Yes! This is worded this way to communicate that K’Sante’s Legend is a passive effect for that turn. This way you can use combat tricks to give that Unit additional Shield, and increase their Assault that turn!
Q: If I pull Neeko and have fewer than 3 Legends, can I still play Neeko?
A: Yes, you can! Neeko is receiving an errata to read “...choose up to 3 different Legends...” so you can still legally play Neeko in Pre-Rift even if you don’t pull 3 Legends.
Q: Can I choose the same option twice when playing Encore?
A: No, you cannot. You must choose 2 different options from the 4.
Q: When an Equipment becomes a unit, does it inherit its equipped text?

A: No. Its “Equipment” text is only active when it is equipped to a unit. If you are running Orianna Legend with a Blade of Exile in your deck and turn it into a Unit, it will be a 3 might Unit without Ganking.
Excited to find a nearby Pre-Rift? Check the event locator and find one near you—and don’t forget to post your hits! Tag us at @PlayRiftbound with the hashtag #RBRadiance.

details.title: OCTOBER 2026 TOURNAMENT RULES CHANGELOG
paragraphs: Vriss here with a new Tournament Rules Update! Today’s rules go into effect with the Radiance Pre-Rift on October 16, 2026.

While this update may look large, it mostly involves cleaning up small mistakes and adding clarity for judges where it was lacking. I’d like to give a huge shoutout to the Riftbound judge community for all the amazing feedback that helped inform this update, especially @benediktwerner for collating a ton of information and sending it our way. Riftbound thrives when we can work with players and judges to provide the best Organized Play experience possible.
For a detailed breakdown of all the changes, see the bulleted list below. For a link to the full Tournament Rules document, look here:

While we’ve come a long way developing and improving the Tournament Rules, we see a need to share more about our philosophy and thought processes behind this document. We’re working on a new companion document for the Tournament Rules which fully breaks down the philosophy and intent behind each rule, especially for the judge perspective. More details to come soon!
Before letting you dive into the nitty gritty, I want to elaborate on Riftbound’s Gameplay Decision policy (509. in the Tournament Rules).

The Gameplay Decisions policy exists to give players some flexibility when making decisions (we are not aiming for an equivalent of chess’ touch-move), but it is not meant to allow players to take back errors once their opponent is required to call information to their attention.
Player A moves their 3 Might unit to a battlefield and passes focus.
Player B indicates their 2 Might unit at that battlefield is now at 4 Might due to their legend, Wuju Bladesman.
Player A can no longer change their decision to move to that battlefield and pass focus.

High Organized Play Level (OPL) Riftbound events have the highest level of competitive integrity, valuing player’s skills and abilities to evaluate the game and make strategically correct tactical decisions. At high OPL, we never want it to feel like you need to play the game for your opponent or get punished for your opponent’s mistakes.
(At casual OPL, allowing an opponent to take back a mistake like this is not required, but it is encouraged for sportsmanship and learning.)
Increased clarity on when players can change gameplay decisions.
Completely reworked Deck Presentation Error remedies to be clearer and better describe their intent, and detail missing Chosen Champions remedies for all OPLs.
Clarified that loops must be fully deterministic and include no random elements. Added examples.
Clarified that knowingly attempting to engage in Improperly Determining a Winner is cheating, increased penalty at Professional OPL.
Further defined Floor Judge responsibility on correcting errors they see, even if they are not called by a player.
Added clarity to when penalties should be upgraded based on being advantageous to the erroring player.
Expanded Facedown Card Error to include when cards illegally leave a facedown zone.
Added Might/Might Bonus to the parts of a card that must remain intact when a card is altered.
Clarified that players are allowed to bluff about their private information.
Clarified that tokens must be represented by card objects with a clear ready state and must be understandable by opponents when used.
Clarified “choosing” things, lethal damage, and adding resources as examples of observable impact for triggers.
Added a requirement for the state of additional turns to be communicated between players.
Clarified that when applying remedies, a “full round cycle” completes when the player whose turn the error occurred on begins their next turn.
Added missing penalties for illegally scouting matches or using electronic devices at inappropriate times.
Clarified that randomized deck checks should occur at the start of a round and should verify all deck elements, added some process clarification.
Corrected typo in Mispayment for Cost remedy.
Clarified that Battlefields can’t be reused if a game loss is applied after Battlefields have been revealed.
Changed the Overpayment for Cost remedies to not include giving the erroring player floating resources if a simple rewind is not possible.
Clarified that players may look at outside notes during sideboarding and after Battlefields are revealed, but must stop once opening hands are drawn (before mulligans).
Clarified that best-of-one sideboarding does not apply to limited competitions.
Clarified Failure to Maintain Game State warnings are fully exempt from upgrades.
Added guidance for judges when performing a shuffle remedy and the deck is fully known or the randomized portion is indeterminable.
Added special deck registration requirements for special deckbuilding rules such as Neeko.
Updated Failure to Maintain Game State to exclude penalties covered by missed triggers.
Updated Chosen Champion sleeve requirements to include secret zones.
Clarified that 1-1 card exchange does not apply to limited sideboarding.
Removed confusing wording that implied deck registration was required at low OPL.
Clarified that at low OPL constructed events, players are typically expected to use the same deck throughout the event, unless given permission otherwise by the tournament organizer.
Clarified that simple rewinds include ready/unrecycling runes spent on the action that is being rewound.

details.title: CORE RULES: RADIANCE PATCH NOTES (EFFECTIVE OCTOBER 16, 2026)
details.tagline: Read about the latest changes to core rules, along with some fun new interactions.
paragraphs: Welcome to the patch notes for Riftbound, Radiance edition. Included in today’s update are rules for playing with Radiance’s new mechanics, updates from the Vendetta FAQ, improvements to the rules’ logical infrastructure to better prepare for future sets and mechanics and a collection of scenarios to help folks understand some of the more complicated interactions introduced with Radiance.

While the patch notes and core rules are aimed at arming our judges, we wanted to include questions and answers prepared by the design team for some of the more tricky interactions and cards released in that set. This article will be released in addition to an FAQ article in the window when we’ve previously released FAQ articles.

Although this article is not an FAQ, it still is a collection of official rulings. These rulings are based on the Core Rules Document that also releases today, as well as the wording of the cards. When a new version of the Core Rules Document is released, it will take precedence over any points that differ from this document.
Throughout this document, we use some specific shorthand to represent symbols in card text. Here’s a short guide:
[C] means “one power of this card’s domain”
[C] in Accelerate costs takes on the domain of the Unit, or turns into [A] if the Unit has no domain or multiple domains.
[C] in other cases is treated as the corresponding power symbol in all respects, matching how the cards are actually printed—it’s just a design shorthand!
What happens when I play Ekko, Boy Who Shattered Time’s activated ability, play a unit, and then play Unlicensed Armoy’s activated ability? Will the unit be killed on my next turn?

Your unit’s death from its triggered ability will be replaced by Unlicensed Armory. Although the unit has the text “Kill me at end of turn.” appended to it, that text is synonymous with “Kill me at the end of this turn.” On subsequent turns, it will not trigger.

When “at end of turn” appears on card text, it is used synonymously with “at the end of this turn.” Although granting that text to a unit is strange, it isn’t outside the bounds of possibility. If the unit remains on the board after the triggered ability resolves, the condition for its ability to trigger will no longer be able to be fulfilled, so it will not trigger again. If the unit changes zones to or from a non-board zone prior to the triggered ability triggering, all of its temporary modifications—including this granted text—will be removed. As such, the ability will no longer exist to trigger.
Can I show off a facedown card at a battlefield with the Show Off ability of Gutter Guardian?
You cannot. Facedown cards don’t have any referenceable characteristics from their front side.

The keyword “Hidden” only appears on the front side of the card; that’s the side with the cost, name, Might, and rules text among other traits. While a card is facedown, any information on its front side cannot be referenced by other cards and effects. Although a facedown card may be friendly to Gutter Guardian, it doesn’t have the appropriate characteristic to be shown off. Note that only the card from hand is revealed with Show Off. You don’t reveal the friendly objects on the board that you’re Showing Off, so you can’t reveal the facedown card even if you wanted to.
What’s up with the reminder text on Chronobreak? Do I get to choose the order?

You get to choose the order if you own all of the units being banished. If you control some number of units that you don’t own and banish those units as well, the units you banish will be placed on the chain starting with units owned by the current turn player and then proceeding in turn order.

Items cannot be placed on the chain simultaneously for any reason. If chain items would be played simultaneously, their controller chooses the order they go on the chain. If multiple players would add items to the chain simultaneously, they place their items on the chain in turn order instead, starting with the current turn player. In the case of Chronobreak, each player chooses the order of their own units being played to the chain (this is what the reminder text is referring to), but each player plays their units to the chain in turn order, starting with the current turn player.

Example: You control five total units, two of which are owned by your opponent. You play Chronobreak, choosing all five units. You banish them, then for each, their owner plays them to the chain as pending items. You’re the current turn player, so you play your three units first in the order of your choice, then your opponent plays their two units in the order of their choice. Pending chain items are finalized from oldest to newest and units resolve as soon as they’re finalized. Thus, we go up the chain starting with the first unit you played to the chain, finalizing and resolving all of the pending units on the chain until there are no more units on the chain. Then we finalize any play effects of those units in the order they triggered. Finally, players can react to the most recent item on the chain. If they don’t, that item resolves, and we repeat the process until all items on the chain have resolved.
What happens when I play Transpositionist’s activated ability choosing an empowered Gangplank, Naval with 6 [M]? Can I play Angler Wyrm?
Gangplank being returned to hand will be replaced with him being given +3 [M] this turn. You can play Angler Wyrm from hand with Transpositionist’s activated ability.

Transpositionist returns a unit to hand and then references that unit’s information. If the unit didn’t change zones and it was a legal target as the instruction that targeted it was being processed, the activated ability will reference that unit’s current information. Gangplank, Naval’s current Might as it is referenced is 9 [M], allowing you to play a unit with 9 [M] or less.
What happens when I choose an attached Equipment with Orianna, Lady of Clockwork?

It detaches from the object it is attached to when it becomes a unit. Although its equip ability can be activated and it can be targeted by Weaponmaster triggers, it cannot attach to a unit; nothing will happen when those abilities resolve.

In this rules update we’ve clarified that units cannot be attached to other game objects. If a unit were to be attached to a game object, it would need to stop being a unit first. If a non-unit game object becomes a unit, it will detach from anything it is attached to as it becomes a unit. If an effect would attempt to attach a unit to another game object without making it no longer a unit first, nothing happens.
What happens when I choose a gear with Deploy located at a battlefield with Orianna, Lady of Clockwork?

That gear will become a unit-gear when the triggered ability resolves; if their controller doesn’t control that battlefield, they will apply contested status to that battlefield, and a combat or showdown will be staged there in the subsequent cleanup. When the chain clears, that showdown or combat will open.

What happens when I choose another gear with Orianna, Lady of Clockwork and the previous unit-gear stops being a unit? Will its attached Equipment fall off? If it’s a deploy gear in base, do I get to move it?
Its attached Equipment will remain attached, and if it is a Deploy gear in base, it will remain in base.

Although units cannot be attached to objects, other objects have no such compunctions. Any attached Equipment that don’t become units will remain attached to the gear even after it stops being a unit. Their Might bonus won’t apply, since the gear doesn’t have a Might, but they will continue to apply their effect text to the gear they are attached to.

The majority of gear with Deploy reference “this battlefield” or “hold here” in such a way that gaining a benefit from base is not possible. That being said, if you want to move it back to a battlefield you can either turn it into a unit again with Orianna, Lady of Clockwork or you can use movement effects that specify moving gear, such as Command: Attack.

Note that there is a small gap between finalizing the Orianna, Lady of Clockwork trigger causing the previous unit-gear to stop being a unit, and the triggered ability resolving and causing the new gear to become a unit. During that gap, neither gear is a unit unless it was already one prior to ever being chosen by Orianna, Lady of Clockwork.

So how does Neeko, Blending In actually work? When do I choose the legends, do I get three legends per Neeko in my deck, can I add multiple of the same legend to the Legend Zone, do the legends enter ready, and do I need to reveal them to my opponent?

You choose the legends during deck building—at competitive OPL, you must register those legends as part of your deck list, and you can store them with your sideboard. The 3 legends are shared by all Neekos in your deck. You cannot add multiple of the same legend to the Legend Zone. The legends enter ready. You do not need to reveal them to your opponent until they are added to the Legend Zone.

Let’s break down Neeko’s rules text. If your deck (Main Deck or sideboard) has one or more copies of Neeko, Blending In, you pick three legends in addition to your starting Champion Legend. Those 3 legends must be different from each other and from your Champion Legend. Regardless of how many copies of Neeko you have in your deck, you will choose three legends in this way.

When Neeko’s play effect resolves, its controller picks one of the legends chosen during deck building and adds it to their Legend Zone alongside their Champion Legend for as long as Neeko is on the board. If Neeko leaves the board, that legend will also cease to exist. The legends don’t exist in any zone of the game while they’re not in the Legend Zone; they don’t exist at all. That being said, if one or more of those legends are already on the board, a player can’t choose to create additional versions of those legends; they can have at most one legend on the board per legend chosen during deckbuilding. If somehow a player played a fourth Neeko, they would fail to add a legend to their legend zone.

The legends added this way are not tokens. They are legend cards and behave in all ways like normal legends do. If an effect instructs a player to “ready a friendly legend” they can target and ready any legends controlled by them or an ally. If an effect instructs a player to ready “your legend,” that refers to any legend controlled by that player. Such an effect does not target a legend; the legend is chosen as the spell or ability resolves.

What happens when the unit on the board that I Showed Off with Primordial Roar is returned to my hand with Star-Crossed? Do I still deal damage? What about if I play Lunar Boon and discard the unit from hand?
You still deal damage in both scenarios.

Any referenced characteristics of shown off objects are locked in when you show them off. Regardless of what subsequently happens to them, their information will be able to be checked by the card that showed them off. This also means that giving a unit +[M] or -[M] after showing that unit off will not affect the damage dealt by Primordial Roar; it’s too late by that point.

What counts as reducing a unit’s Might for Ahri, Confident? If I play Discipline on my 1 [M] unit while it’s stunned and located at the same battlefield as an enemy Leona, Zealot, will I trigger their Ahri, Confident located at that battlefield?

Reducing a unit’s Might means an ability of an object you control causes a unit to receive a -[M] effect. Ahri, Confident will trigger if you Discipline a stunned 1 [M] unit at the same battlefield as an enemy Leona, Zealot.

Although Discipline never causes the unit’s Might to increase, the unit goes from 1 [M] with a -0 [M] effect applied to it, which will not trigger Ahri, Confident, to 3 [M] with a -2 [M] effect applied to it. This change in state triggers Ahri, Confident, the same as a 3 [M] unit being stunned and receiving a -2 [M] effect from Leona, Zealot’s passive ability. Note that this doesn’t work for other cases: if a stunned 3 [M] unit at the same battlefield as an enemy Leona, Zealot has Discipline played on it, that unit will not have a new Might reduction effect applied to it and thus Ahri, Confident will not trigger. Spells, triggered abilities, and activated abilities are easier; if a spell, triggered ability, or activated ability applies non-zero -[M] to a unit, Ahri, Confident will trigger.

The Unleashed and Vendetta rules updates have laid a relatively stable base for this rules update. We’ve made small changes as necessary, but we have fewer logical holes to patch, and there aren’t any sweeping fixes that need to be implemented in this set. The vast majority of the rules in this update are about new cards and mechanics in the Radiance set.
Now let’s take a look at the rules changes we have in store for Radiance!
Deploy is a new keyword appearing on gear in Radiance. Gear with Deploy enable players to apply localized, battlefield-altering effects.
Gear with Deploy can be played to any battlefield; enemy occupied, friendly, or uncontrolled. However, when an opponent holds a battlefield where you have gear with Deploy, those gear will be killed.
Gear with Deploy remain at their current battlefield so long as they aren’t destroyed. Some effects can move gear with Deploy to other battlefields too!
Disarm is a new keyword appearing on units in Radiance.

Disarm is an attack trigger. The first time a unit with Disarm attacks each combat, they will give an enemy unit at their battlefield -1 [M] this turn. If a unit has Disarm 2, they’ll give an enemy unit -2 [M] this turn.

Disarm stacks just like Assault or Shield; meaning if a unit has gained multiple Disarm keywords from different sources, the unit will have one trigger for Disarm with a total of the sum of their Disarm values.
Show Off is a new keyword appearing on both units and spells in Radiance.
When you Show Off something, you reveal a card from your hand that matches the requirement, or pick a friendly game object (card or token) on the board with the appropriate characteristics.
Cards with Show Off can reference information from the shown off card or object. That information is locked in when the card or object is shown off, even if it’s referenced later.
NEW RULE: Show Off keyword added.

We saw some confusion on how copy effects work and their placement in the trait-altering layer. In the Radiance rules update, we’ve moved to clarify this by giving copy effects a layer of their own. The first layer is now for copy effects and all subsequent layers (trait-altering, ability-altering, arithmetic) have been shifted down to reflect this change.

Because copy effects only interacted with other copy effects anyway, there was functionally no reason for them to remain in the trait-altering layer. Our hope with this move is that it will be clearer that they only interact with other copy effects. Effects like the Mech tag appended by Experimental Hexplate in the trait-altering layer are not copied by copy effects.
NEW RULE: Copy Effects layer added.
To support and build on this clarification for copy effects, we’ve also added the copy game action to the game actions section.

This section also clarifies how game objects that are created as copies, like the tokens played by Zilean, Time Mage’s replacement effect, work; those game objects don’t have a copy effect applied to them, but are created directly with the copyable traits of the object it is a copy of, as if those were its own printed traits.
NEW RULE: Copy game action added.
Radiance’s Neeko, Blending In adds the first instance of additional choices made during deckbuilding, so we’ve added rules to clarify how those choices are made.
NEW RULE: Additional deckbuilding decisions added.

Orianna, Lady of Clockwork presents some unique rules scenarios for the game, including what happens to an Equipment that becomes a unit. We decided on the simplest answer: units can’t be attached to other game objects. If an attached game object becomes a unit, it detaches immediately.
CLARIFIED RULE: Units cannot be attached to other game objects.
CLARIFIED RULE: If an attached non-unit game object becomes a unit, it detaches as it becomes a unit.
Rules Update: Layer Calculations and Object Dependencies
We’ve added rules for layer calculations in an effort to support future interactions and clarify how the layer effects are calculated.

When calculating layer effects, each game object is treated individually. If a game object needs to reference information from another game object, the game evaluates that game object’s layer information before returning to calculate the original game object’s information.
If multiple game objects reference information from each other, instead evaluate all of their information simultaneously, layer by layer.
NEW RULE: Layer calculation procedure added.

We’re starting to see the word “pick” appear on cards, which will become even more important when Legacy releases early next year. Pick is the word we’re moving towards for when you make a choice that isn’t a target. We want to make it clear to players that when a card says for you to  “choose” something, that means you are targeting what you choose.

When the Legacy rules and templating change is implemented in card text, many cards that currently say “choose” will have their text updated to pick. We are doing some of that work in Radiance. As such, we can also make this clearer in the rules prior to the Legacy rules update.
In Vendetta we saw some players understandably confused over the scope of conditional clauses in instruction text.
With the Radiance rules update, we’ve clarified what scope conditional clauses have in a given instruction.
NEW RULE: Conditional clauses scope added.
Rules Update: Finalizing Time Actions Scope

We received feedback that cards which referred to “you” when checking if costs were paid or actions were taken was confusing if control of the card is gained by another player. New rules have been added to clarify this.
NEW RULE: Instructions of a spell or ability may reference actions taken during Finalization. They will do so by checking whether “you” performed those game actions.

NEW RULE: These instructions check whether the game action was performed, not by whom. If another player gains control of the spell or ability after the game action was performed during finalization, it will still be considered true for the purposes of these instructions.

In the Vendetta rules update we included a model for making new choices as used by cards like Mystic Reversal and Rebuttal. We received feedback that the rules were unclear, and we clarified in the Vendetta FAQ how the interim model would work. Upon review, we found we weren’t entirely satisfied with that implementation.  We decided to overhaul how new decisions are made to be simpler and more intuitive.
When making new decisions now, all decisions must be made anew. You can choose to make the same decisions as made previously, but if you’re making new decisions, you can’t go halfway.

Similar to the previous model, all decisions must be legal and valid; however, with this new model, any abilities that trigger on targeting, for example, will trigger again; even if you previously targeted the same unit. It should feel like you’re going through the process of choosing targets all over again.
CLARIFIED RULE: Making new choices updated.
Rules Update: Pending Item Target Legality

Players have long wondered whether pending items are legal to target with spells and abilities. It’s very rare that such a case is possible but, like many strange rules interactions in Riftbound, we can blame these few cases on Promising Future. We figured we might as well make it clear: Pending items are not legal targets for spells and abilities.
NEW RULE: Pending item target legality clarified.

The rules for 2v2 scoring were slightly contradictory. In the Vendetta rules update we cleaned them up, and in this rules update they’ve been fully aligned. Specifically, the final point and scoring eligibility special rules now apply only to teams that maintain control of a battlefield during their own or a teammate’s turn, and not during an opponent’s turn.
Vendetta’s Kayle, Justified needed some support from the FAQ. We’ve codified that support with the Radiance rules update.

NEW RULE: Game Objects with Empower abilities may have or gain permissions to be Empowered multiple times. Such Game Objects ignore the normal “Play only if not Empowered.” restriction on Empower abilities.
Note that this means you can activate the ability even if you’re at your max number of empowered statuses. That is intentional! It just does nothing. That is also intentional.

Insightful judges and players recognized some strangeness in the rules for linked instructions from the Unleashed rules update, made more apparent by rules added in the Vendetta rules update. In the Vendetta FAQ we clarified how those rules should function, and now we’re codifying that fix into the Radiance rules update.

If an instruction mistargets, that instruction is ignored. If an instruction fails to execute for any other reason, such as it being replaced, skipped, or being impossible to perform, it is negated. Instructions that are ignored will cause any later instructions linked to them to also be ignored. If an instruction is negated, later linked instructions will not be negated; they will still execute if possible.
NEW RULE: Negated and ignored instructions added.

The Vendetta FAQ clarified how Dragon Roost and other mandatory requirements functioned together. We’ve codified that into the rules in the Radiance rules update with extra clarifications. We’ve also codified the concept of a restriction: that being an effect like Perched Grimwyrm’s “Play me only to a battlefield you’ve conquered this turn.”

As we’ve shared before, we’re preparing a major update to Riftbound rules with Legacy in January. To part the curtain some, this is a massive undertaking—we’re completely reformatting the rules documents to improve their readability as reference for players and judges.
We’re literally starting from the ground up, which will give us room to reduce redundant information, improve ordering, and generally clean up the rules documentation.
To be clear: this is about rewriting the rules to be more readable, and it won’t change how Riftbound’s mechanics actually work.
As always, we do not update the rules of Riftbound or introduce card errata to manage the power level of any card or effect—if we ever need to manage a powerful card, we’ll use other tools.
We’ll release an additional FAQ article after Radiance is released to further clarify remaining points of confusion for players and keep you updated as we learn more.

details.title: RIFTBOUND PREMIER PLAY: EARLY 2027 EVENTS
details.tagline: The first locations and dates for the 2027 Riftbound Regionals and Riftbound Continental are here!
paragraphs: As promised in our State of Play we dropped earlier this year, we’ve got the new dates and locations for the next Continental and Regionals. The full overview of premier play isn’t quite ready, but we wanted to get you dates for the start of 2027 as early as possible so you can begin planning appropriately.
With that said, let’s jump right into the events for the first release of 2027: Set 6, Legacy.
Note: We have one more Regional coming to the Oceania region during the Legacy season, once details are locked we will update this article.
These are what you know and love as RQ’s, but we’re streamlining the naming!
If you’re just joining us, here’s a recap on what Regionals are all about:
Regionals are three-day-events with two different badge types, Competitor and Attendee.
Competitor Badge holders can enter the main event running on Day 2 and Day 3, to battle it out for Foil Plated Legends as well as other top-cut goodies including a Continental invite.
Attendee Badge holders can participate in side events, catch merch drops, and community activities to entertain you even if you aren’t participating in the main event.

Our first continental will bring us to Dallas, Texas in the heart of the United States. As a reminder, Riftbound Continentals will be the spiritual successor to the Regional Championships we’re holding this year, but they’re different in a few important ways:
Rather than occurring at the end of the year, we will hold Continentals throughout the year with a Continental tied to each set and hosted in a city, rotating around the world.

The Continental tournaments are three-days, with day one being an open entry qualifier for those who don’t yet have their invite to the main event which begins on Saturday. This means everyone has an opportunity to compete in the main event at the Continental.
For those who don’t play in the main event, there will still be lots of side events as well as chances to meet creators and members of the Riftbound team throughout the weekends.
As we get closer to the events themselves, keep an eye on our official channels to get updates on the full schedule and details of each event.

That’s all for today! Don’t forget to use the above hashtags to share your excitement pre and post events. We know you probably still have questions about our plans for the rest of Organized Play, we will be back in the next few months with a deeper dive into what’s changing for all of that and more.
Until then, go sling some cards and support your local game shops.

details.title: SEPTEMBER BAN LIST UPDATES (EFFECTIVE SEPTEMBER 18, 2026)
details.tagline: We’re announcing the latest cards added to the Standard and Constructed 2v2 ban list.
paragraphs: Two cards are being added to the Standard and 2v2 Constructed ban list:

With the Shenyang Regional Open completed and the Los Angeles Regional Qualifier on the horizon, we wanted to release these bans quickly to let people adjust as we head into the Regional Championships. With this in mind, we’re publishing this article first in English and will translate it for other languages as soon as possible.
As we’ve previously discussed, there are three questions we ask when considering whether to ban a card:
Is this card overrepresented in an unhealthy way?
Are the problems with this card likely to get better or worse over time?
Does this card promote unhealthy play patterns?

Since the emergence of the Lux combo deck in Unleashed, we’ve been monitoring its tournament representation and performance. Although the play rate has remained low, we believe this style of infinite promotes an unhealthy play pattern due to its limited windows of interaction and solitaire-esque gameplay required to execute the combo. The design of Ekko is unique in that it both effectively grants an extra turn and also recycles itself, and in retrospect the benefits of a risky exciting effect that's resonant to Ekko's identity didn't outweigh the dangers of the infinites he enabled. Considering how the strategy has developed and that banning it shouldn’t affect most other Mind decks, we’ve decided to act now. A match of Riftbound should be a fun and interactive experience for both players, and this change should help ensure that.

Stacked Deck is a low opportunity cost inclusion in a decklist that provides general consistency as well as cheap synergy when combined with cards like Ravenbloom Student or Battlefields like Abandoned Hall. While we acknowledge that the card is fun to play and can slot into any Chaos strategy seamlessly, the consistency it provides is higher than we would like and has shown a compounding issue with the release of the Kennen legend.  When combined with Lightning Rush, this card lets Kennen churn through the deck a little too efficiently, finding key cards like Nocturne while simultaneously filling the trash for Rhasa the Sunderer and Last Rites.

We think Kennen will feel the loss of Stacked Deck acutely, as his current strategy is built around maximizing card selection and having less access to it will slow down the entire engine. Without Stacked Deck as an autoinclude in most Chaos decklists, we’re excited to see the adaptation in deckbuilding that players make.

We’ve been carefully monitoring the win rates of decks in our major tournaments as well as general community sentiment around the current metagame. For everyone that’s talked to us and shared opinions, we hear you, and genuinely appreciate your passion. The Riftbound community is truly great, and we’re committed to working with players to make the best decisions we can for the health of the game.

We want to avoid having a definitive best deck in the format. Kennen’s play rate and win rate warrant a targeted ban that doesn’t obliterate the deck and strategy, but brings it more in line with other top decks. We think the Stacked Deck ban will leave the core strategy intact but make it less consistent and less powerful overall.  We recognize this will have knock-on effects on the rest of the metagame, but we’re confident that it will put us into the best position for the future of the game as we head into the Los Angeles Regional Qualifier and the Chengdu Major.

details.title: INTRODUCING THE NEW PLAYRIFTBOUND.COM
details.tagline: Check out new tools for finding, attending, and running Organized Play events on September 14.
paragraphs: On September 14, 2026, PlayRiftbound.com will become the home of Riftbound Organized Play.
Here’s the TLDR on what you need to know about the update:
Starting with Radiance Pre-Rift registration, players and stores will use PlayRiftbound.com instead of carde.io to find, register for, play at, and run events.
Players will sign in with their Riot ID, with no account linking required.
If you don’t have a Riot account, create one before registration opens.
We’re building this platform from the ground up, so we’re prioritizing the most important features for Organized Play before expanding what PlayRiftbound.com can do.
Let us know what you'd like to see in future updates!

Beginning September 14, 2026, PlayRiftbound.com will be updated with built-in features for finding and registering for events. It will also be the new home for match pairings and recording results during an event.

You’ll still find the Rules Hub and new Riftbound articles on the site, and some sections will have a new look and feel. Most importantly, we’ll introduce new tournament tools for players and stores. Overall, it’ll be easier to find (or create) a place to play Riftbound in your local area.

Carde.io, the current site for Organized Play events, has been an excellent partner during Riftbound’s launch. We’re switching to PlayRiftbound.com, a Riot-owned website, because many of our ideas for Riftbound’s future would benefit from an internal platform or require one.
Plus, PlayRiftbound.com uses Riot IDs for sign-ins and registrations, which means that you’ll no longer need to go through an account-linking process to access Organized Play.

We’re moving to a completely new home base for Organized Play, but using it should feel pretty familiar. Whether you’re new to Riftbound or you’ve been to tons of events before, here’s what to do when you visit PlayRiftbound.com for the first time.
Sign in with your existing Riot account, or create one through the Riot account page.
Starting with Radiance Pre-Rift registration, use the updated event search to find a place to play near you.
Register for your chosen event with your Riot ID; no account linking is required.
Once you’re playing at the event, use your phone to check pairings and record your results.

PlayRiftbound.com is also being built for the stores and organizers who create local Riftbound play. At launch, stores will have one place to support event registration and help players find their events, and sign-ups should have fewer account issues. We want stores and their teams to have good experiences when it comes to making and running our events whether it’s a weekly Nexus Night, a Pre-Rift, or a future event such as the Nexus Cup and Challenge Series.
We want to make it easier to create great experiences for players.

We’ll be back with more about the new programs for stores in an update at the end of October. That update will be the follow-up to our State of Play article where we gave a full picture of the Riftbound Organized Play system in 2027.
We aren’t announcing development timelines for PlayRiftbound.com updates yet, but here are some of the improvements we’re already exploring to support play programs in 2027.
Better tools for tournament organizers and judges running local events, large tournaments, and side events.
More ways to compete, including expanded 2v2 tournament support.
Easier decklist creation and validation across competitive formats.
Improvements for finding and viewing Riftbound cards.
We’re planning to share semi-regular updates about what we’re working on, big or small, to keep players up to date. Keep an eye on the News page for future announcements.
Q: Will my play history be lost from carde.io?
No. We’re working with UVS and carde.io to migrate player history to the new platform.
Q: Various Riftbound fan projects rely on carde.io data. Will the new site continue enabling them?

The short answer is that those projects will likely be interrupted by this change, but it’s not our goal to break these sites. We’d love to keep seeing a vibrant offering of community-created tools for playing Riftbound, so long as they abide by the developer agreements and guidelines regarding community projects.
Q: I’m a store owner and haven’t received transition information. What should I do?
Reach out to your UVS or regional store partner, and they’ll guide you through the steps to move your store to the new platform.
Q: How can I share ideas and feedback?
We’ll be watching social media carefully for issues that arise, as well as awesome ideas from the community on how to make PlayRiftbound.com even better.
